paper_metadata.title: Large Language Models for Automatic Knowledge Graph Construction From Text Documents: a Materials Science Case Study
paper_metadata.venue: Digital Transformation and Intelligent Systems: Theory, Models, Practice (monograph)
paper_metadata.abstract: The study compares GPT-4, Qwen, and DeepSeek for automated generation of OWL ontologies from materials-science articles. It finds that prompt engineering and iterative refinement can produce basic ontologies, but depth, accuracy, and scalability remain inadequate for fully automatic construction.

problem_addressed: How to use general LLMs to turn a materials-science research article into a valid, populated OWL ontology/knowledge-graph representation, and which model and prompting strategy yields the most complete and linked result. The study specifically tests whether prompt detail and staged generation mitigate the difficulty of creating logically consistent, domain-specific ontologies.

methodology.primary_family: Zero-shot and few-shot LLM prompting (without task-specific model training)
methodology.description: Contributions and workflow: (1) compares GPT-4, four Qwen variants, and DeepSeek-R1 on OWL generation from materials-science PDF articles; (2) designs and iteratively refines prompts from a general request (P1), through an explicit domain ontology schema (P2), to DeepSeek's staged creation/augmentation workflow (P3); (3) asks models to identify article metadata, authors, materials, processes, methods, properties, figures, results, and references; classify them as OWL classes/individuals; and emit RDF/XML OWL with object and data properties; (4) loads/parses outputs with Jena-Fuseki and Protégé, executes SPARQL count queries, and compares triples, classes, properties, individuals, and linkage factors. Author-reported conclusion: staged DeepSeek-R1 is the best current approach in this study, but remains a human-supervised assistant rather than an autonomous ontology generator.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: OWL/RDF ontology is both the target representation and a prompt-specified schema. P2 supplies classes and expected properties for article, abstract, author, material, research method, process, material property, structural component, and results/findings; models may add classes/properties. DeepSeek P3 explicitly constructs the class hierarchy before object properties, datatype properties, and named individuals.

input_output.input_type: PDF text of materials-science scientific research articles, including article sections, figures and captions, and bibliography/references.
input_output.input_granularity: One full scientific article PDF per model interaction in the main experiment; an additional materials-science article is tested with Qwen. The requested ontology spans document-level metadata, figures, technical terms, references, and research content.
input_output.output_representation: OWL ontology, principally RDF/XML, containing OWL classes, named individuals, object properties, datatype properties, RDF triples, labels/comments, and optionally domains/ranges; intended to be usable by a graph DBMS.

datasets: Main input: one unpublished experimental materials-science research article on alumomatrix composites Al-Si-Ni and Al-TiC and their coefficient of thermal expansion.
Additional Qwen test: “Al-Si-Ni SINTERED ALLOY: STRUCTURE AND PROPERTIES. PART 2: SINTERING AND FORGING.”

metrics: Average object properties per named individual
Average datatype properties per named individual
Qualitative completeness, correctness, depth, coherence, and scalability assessment
baselines: Bare demonstration ontology: 21 RDF triples, 5 classes, 3 object properties, 2 datatype properties, and no named individuals.
Comparative prompt/model conditions: GPT-4 P1/P2/P2-extended, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct P1/P2/P2-article 2, and DeepSeek-R1 P3.
evaluation.setting: Small exploratory case study using one common PDF for the main model comparisons because of Qwen's one-file-per-message restriction and input/output limits. Prompt P1 is simple, P2 gives a detailed ontology structure, and P3 uses step-by-step entity creation and augmentation. Generated OWL is parsed/loaded and assessed with Jena-Fuseki, Protégé, SPARQL structural queries, and qualitative manual inspection. No gold-standard ontology exists, so no precision/recall or task-accuracy evaluation is performed.

value: Table 10.2: GPT-4 P1 produced 54 triples/14 classes/5 OP/8 DP/7 named individuals; GPT-4 P2 produced 107/14/10/8/47; GPT-4 P2-extended produced 128/14/11/8/22.
Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct P1 was invalid; P2 produced 236 triples/8 classes/9 OP/14 DP/27 named individuals; P2 on article 2 produced 262/9/26/0/45.
DeepSeek-R1 P3 produced the largest artifact: 878 triples, 55 classes, 30 OP, 12 DP, 68 named individuals, 3.02 average OP/NI, and 1.89 average DP/NI.

Author interpretation: DeepSeek's staged workflow yielded the most detailed and coherent ontology among the tested conditions, whereas GPT-4 and Qwen were not strong candidates for complete automatic OWL-ontology generation.

code_and_data_availability: The paper provides links to the main unpublished input PDF and a second test article on Google Drive, and cites public GitHub Gists for GPT-4 demonstration ontologies, Qwen-generated artifacts/responses, and a DeepSeek-generated OWL ontology. No consolidated code repository, executable experiment scripts, prompt archive, or complete reproducibility package is reported in the paper.
